title: GOLOG
summary:
GOLOG is a high-level logic programming language for the specification and execution of complex actions in dynamical domains. It is based on the situation calculus and is a first-order logical language for reasoning about action and change. GOLOG was developed at the University of Toronto.

A procedural programming language like C defines the execution of statements in advance, where the programmer creates a subroutine which consists of statements and the computer executes each statement in a linear order. In contrast, fifth-generation programming languages like Golog work with an abstract model with which the interpreter can generate the sequence of actions. The source code defines the problem and it is up to the solver to find the next action.

This approach can facilitate the management of complex problems from the domain of robotics. A Golog program defines the state space in which the agent is allowed to operate, and a path in the symbolic domain is found with state space search. To speed up the process, Golog programs are realized as hierarchical task networks. The ConGolog language extension provides concurrency and interrupts.

Golog has been used to model the behavior of autonomous agents. It enables the construction of complex actions using typical programming language constructs and is used for applications in high-level control of robots and industrial processes, virtual agents, discrete event simulation, and more. It can also be used to develop Belief Desire Intention-style agent systems. In contrast to the Planning Domain Definition Language, Golog supports planning and scripting as well. The foundational paper was authored by Hector J. Levesque, Raymond Reiter, Yves Lesperance, Fangzhen Lin, and Richard B. Scherl, with a prototype implementation in Prolog.
